keep: He never said the line about suckers. What he did say, in his own book, is that everything depended on getting people to talk.
lede: The line everyone knows him by was pinned on him after he died. What he did do is worse. In 1835 he paid $1,000 to exhibit an enslaved old woman as George Washington's 161-year-old nurse, and when she died he sold tickets to her dissection.
copy: His father died in 1825, when he was fifteen, and the estate could not pay half its debts. He clerked in a store, ran lotteries to clear the shop-worn stock, and started a weekly in Danbury, The Herald of Freedom. He was prosecuted for libel three times in three years. The third time, for printing that a Bethel churchman had taken usury of an orphan boy, he got a $100 fine and sixty days in the county jail. His room there was papered and carpeted. He edited the paper from it, and a band played him home. In 1835 he was offered the exhibition of Joice Heth, advertised as a woman of 161 who had belonged to Washington's father. He had $500, borrowed $500 more, and sold his share of a grocery. She died the next February. On 25 February 1836 the surgeon David L. Rogers cut her open in New York's City Saloon in front of 1,500 paying spectators, and found she was nowhere near the age on the posters. Barnum's own book covers it in a clause: the doctors disagreed.

The method was to make people argue, and it scaled. He opened the American Museum on Broadway in 1841. In 1850 he authorised his agent to offer Jenny Lind up to $1,000 a night for as many as 150 nights, and deposited $187,500 with her London bankers before she sailed. A lender laughed in his face and said he would never take $3,000 at a single concert. The first one, at Castle Garden, took $17,864. The tour ran to 95 concerts and $712,161; Lind's share came to $176,675 and his gross, after paying her, to $535,486. Five years later he lent his name as security for $110,000 to the Jerome Clock Company. It kept drawing on him past that, and in 1856 he signed over everything he owned to his creditors. He opened his circus in Brooklyn on 10 April 1871, at sixty.

"There's a sucker born every minute" is the part that is wrong. Quote Investigator traced the family of sayings back to 1806, through a 'flat' born every minute in 1835, and found the 'sucker' version first in a Chicago paper in 1879, as an anonymous gamblers' adage. Before Barnum it was credited to Hungry Joe, to Artemus Ward and to Mike McDonald. A Chicago advertisement first gave a version to Barnum in 1890, with 'fool'; the 'sucker' line reached him in a Victoria newspaper in July 1892, fifteen months after he died. The tale that a rival showman said it of Barnum's crowds at the Cardiff Giant has no document behind it either. His record on race does: the man who sold tickets to Joice Heth's autopsy stood up in the Connecticut legislature on 26 May 1865 and argued that the state's white voters should be asked to give Black men the vote.

bio.t: P. T. Barnum: The Legend and the Man
bio.why: Saxon edited Barnum's selected letters (1983) before he wrote the life, so it is built from the papers and not from the autobiography, which Barnum rewrote and reissued himself. For Joice Heth the book to read is Benjamin Reiss's The Showman and the Slave (2001); for why the crowds paid to be fooled, Neil Harris's Humbug (1973).

contested: Whether he knew. Barnum's own account makes him a buyer who took the papers at face value (everything, he says, seemed so straightforward), and he is the only witness to his own good faith. The account from outside his is Benjamin Reiss's The Showman and the Slave (2001); this entry has not opened it and does not say what it concludes, but a reader of the 1872 edition should notice that its handling of the autopsy is one clause long. The 1865 speech cuts both ways. It argues that a soul is immortal whatever body it lives in, a long way from his 1835 handbills; it also asks only that Connecticut's white voters be allowed to decide, the narrowest form the question could take. On the famous line, the sources agree it is not his. Nobody has produced a document for the Cardiff Giant story, and the Law Library of Congress, asked in 2011 for a court record of it, could say only that David Hannum may or may not have said it.
